# Program *Bridge*
## End-of-Life and Migration Program for Platform L → Platform N

**Program envelope:** 60 months of active program (M−6 → M54), with residual bridge-component obligations extending to ~M78. Public customer-facing headline: *"Platform L is supported through M42; a limited, paid, plan-gated extension path exists to M54."*

> **Working assumptions — replace with your actuals.** All figures below labeled *(illustrative)* are placeholders whose purpose is to show the model structure and force the arithmetic to close. The decision logic holds regardless of the inputs.
>
> | Input | Assumption *(illustrative)* |
> |---|---|
> | Platform L revenue | $260M/yr; contribution profit $150M ≈ 33% of company profit |
> | Accounts on L | ~4,000, of which ~40 "Strategic" accounts = ~55% of L revenue |
> | Deployment mix | 45% vendor-hosted, 50% customer on-prem, 5% air-gapped/regulated |
> | OEM/embedded partners | 14 partners, ~6% of L revenue, ~900 downstream end-customers |
> | Sustaining cost | ~$28M/yr, growing 10–15%/yr |
> | Key-person exposure | 9 engineers hold sole ownership of L subsystems; 4 retire within 36 months |

---

# 1. Strategic options: why sunset, and what stays on the table

The board will ask why we are not simply keeping or selling L. The plan must show the comparison.

| Option | Description | NPV *(illustrative, 7-yr)* | Security liability | Customer relationship | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Sunset & migrate** (recommended) | Publish EOL, rebuild the load-bearing capabilities on N, fund migration | **+$310M** | Extinguished by M42/M54 | Preserved if executed well; ~8–12% churn expected | **Adopt** |
| **B. Divest / license L** to a specialist maintenance roll-up | Carve out code, contracts, and 2–3 sustaining engineers; buyer supports the tail | +$150M to +$240M (high variance) | **Transferred** — the single largest benefit | Relationship intermediated; N cross-sell rights must be contractually reserved | **Reject as the whole answer; retain as a live option for the residual tail (see §1.1)** |
| **C. Reprice and hold** — fund L via 2–3× maintenance uplift, no sunset | Keep L indefinitely, self-funded | −$40M to +$90M, degrading | **Retained and compounding** | Buys 24–36 months of peace, then a worse version of the same crisis with fewer engineers and a hostile installed base | **Reject** (documented as baseline) |

**Why A over C:** repricing does not buy engineers who no longer exist, and it does not remove the unpatchable-dependency risk. It converts an operational problem into an existential one on a delay.

**Why A over B outright:** B forfeits the ~85% of L revenue that is migratable to N, and a roll-up buyer's incentive is to harvest, not to keep our customers warm for N. Divesting the *whole* base sells our own future revenue at a discount.

### 1.1 The hybrid: reserve B for the residual

At the **M30 gate (G4)** we will know the size of the irreducible residue — accounts that cannot or will not migrate (air-gapped, regulated-frozen, acquired, contractually locked). Two paths:

- Residue **< ~2% of L revenue** → run Custom Support Agreements to M54 in-house.
- Residue **> ~2%** → execute a **carve-out transfer** of that segment (code branch + contracts + a small sustaining team) to a specialist provider, with a reserved right of re-approach for N. This is strictly better than running an in-house museum staffed by contractors.

**Action now:** run a quiet market-sounding of 3–4 maintenance roll-up buyers during Phase 0 so the option is priced, not theoretical, when G4 arrives.

---

# 2. Operating principles

1. **You cannot keep L.** The cost curve compounds, the knowledge base is evaporating, and unpatchable upstream dependencies convert a financial problem into an existential one. Time is not neutral; waiting is the expensive option.
2. **You cannot force-march the top accounts.** They are a third of the profit and they have credible alternatives. A migration experienced as coercion converts a support problem into a competitive loss.
3. **Job parity, not feature parity.** Rebuild the *outcomes* a handful of loyal customers depend on; be ruthless about the long tail of toggles nobody uses.
4. **Published dates; capped, priced, plan-gated exceptions; no free extensions.**
   *(This replaces the seductive but dishonest slogan "dates never slip." Our dates* can *move: earlier under the security tripwire (§4.4), later only via a paid, approval-gated, individually capped Custom Support Agreement that requires a signed migration completion date. We say this out loud on day one, because sophisticated procurement will work it out in the first hour and we would rather be trusted than clever.)*
5. **Commitments before deadlines.** We publish the parity commitments and the tooling roadmap *at the same moment* as the shutoff calendar — never the deadline first.
6. **Early is cheapest, and that never reverses.** Incentives decay on a published schedule and are never improved retroactively for latecomers (§7.4). The first time we hold this line under pressure is the moment the whole program becomes credible.

---

# 3. Phase 0 — Discovery, instrumentation, and readiness (M−6 → M0)

**Nothing is announced until Gate G0 passes.** An EOL date announced without usage data, a parity commitment, and a sustaining plan is how you lose your top ten accounts in one quarter.

| # | Workstream | Output | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Usage telemetry / fingerprinting | Per-account, per-feature, per-API usage map; ≥85% of L installs instrumented (on-prem: opt-in agent, log ingest, or funded audit) | Eng + Data |
| 2 | Feature census | Every capability, flag, endpoint, report, export format, connector — with active-user counts and revenue attachment | Product |
| 3 | **Dependency EOL calendar** (§4.5) | Every OS, DB, runtime, crypto library, browser, appliance, and third-party component mapped to *its own* vendor EOL date against M0–M54 | Platform Eng + Security |
| 4 | Account segmentation & defection risk model | Tier assignment (§7.1) + risk scores (§8.1) | Sales Ops + CS |
| 5 | Cost-of-carry model | True annual L cost incl. security, infra, insurance loading, and opportunity cost of engineers | Finance |
| 6 | **Key-person / knowledge asset audit** | Subsystems with fewer than two competent owners; retirement dates; sustaining plan inputs (§5) | Eng leadership |
| 7 | Legal review | Contract-by-contract: perpetual licenses, evergreen support commitments, notice periods, OEM/embedded rights, regulated obligations, MFN clauses, termination-for-convenience terms | Legal |
| 8 | Competitive intel & switching-cost model | Rival migration offers, poaching targets, realistic TCO of switching to a competitor | Product Marketing |
| 9 | Divest option sounding | Indicative pricing from 3–4 maintenance roll-ups (§1.1) | Corp Dev |
| 10 | Financial model & investor narrative | Profit bridge, guidance treatment (§6) | CFO + IR |

### 3.1 Cover narrative and leak plan

Six months of instrumentation, funded audits, and contract review across 4,000 accounts and a field organization **will leak.** Plan for it rather than pretending otherwise.

- **Honest public framing from M−6:** *"We are running a Platform Modernization Assessment across our product line to plan the next decade of investment."* This is true, non-deniable-later, and consistent with the eventual announcement.
- **Leak-response kit ready at M−6:** pre-drafted holding statement, field FAQ, and an accelerated Tier 1 briefing sequence that can be triggered within 48 hours. If a credible leak occurs, we **pull the announcement forward** rather than deny it. Denial is the one action that cannot be recovered from.
- **Field discipline:** no rep is briefed on the EOL decision before M−1. Reps are given a truthful, sufficient answer for the assessment framing. Anyone who speculates on dates is corrected in writing.
- **Gate G0 exit criteria (see §11.2)** include "leak-response kit tested" and "Tier 1 briefing calendar locked."

---

# 4. Sunset timeline and support policy

## 4.1 The single support & price ladder

One table. This supersedes any prior pricing statements and is published as a versioned policy document that becomes the contractual reference.

| State | Window | **Hosted L** | **On-prem L** | Price (× current effective maintenance) | Included | Excluded |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Full Support** | M0 → M18 | Yes | Yes | **1.0×** (price-locked for accounts on a signed migration plan) | Security patches, Sev-1→4 fixes, dependency compatibility certifications, migration-blocker fixes, full SLAs | New features (frozen M0) |
| **Maintenance Support** | M18 → M30 | Yes | Y

Past monetization tests backfired: aggressive paywalls spiked uninstalls, and intrusive ads damaged app-store ratings within weeks. Usage data shows several distinct user segments that get very different value from the product.

Design a monetization strategy that meaningfully increases revenue per user while protecting retention and ratings. Choose and justify the mix of subscription tiers, usage-based pricing, advertising, and partnerships; map offers to the identified user segments; and define the experiment plan and guardrail metrics that will catch churn damage before it compounds.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

# Program *Ratchet*
## Monetization Architecture for a Free-Majority Consumer App

**Envelope:** 24 months to durable positive contribution, structured as four release waves (W1–W4) behind five decision gates (G0–G4).
**Naming rationale:** a ratchet turns one way. Every monetization move must *add* a reason to pay; we never re-price a habit the user already has. That single constraint is what separates this plan from the two tests that backfired.

> **Working assumptions — replace with your actuals.** Everything labeled *(illustrative)* is a placeholder that exists to make the model structure legible and force the arithmetic to close. The decision logic is invariant to the inputs.
>
> | Input | Assumption *(illustrative)* |
> |---|---|
> | MAU / DAU | 8.0M / 2.1M (DAU:MAU 26%) |
> | Paid conversion | 1.8% of MAU = ~144k subscribers |
> | Current pricing | $6.99/mo, $49.99/yr; 55/45 monthly/annual mix |
> | Current revenue | ~$8.2M ARR (≈$1.02 ARPMAU/yr, ≈$0.085/mo) |
> | Cost base | ~$19M/yr → ~$11M/yr burn |
> | Investor requirement | Credible path to breakeven inside 18 months, positive by M24 |
> | Store fee (blended) | 18–22% (mix of 30% year-one, 15% post-year-one and small-business tiers) |
> | Ratings position | 4.4★ iOS / 4.2★ Android; prior ad test cost ~0.4★ in 5 weeks |
> | Prior test damage | Paywall test: uninstalls +19% in exposed cohort; ads test: 1★ share 2.1× baseline |

---

# 1. Diagnosis: why the previous two tests failed

This is not optional preamble. If we do not name the failure mechanism precisely, we will rebuild it with better UI.

| Failed test | What we did | Why it backfired | Structural lesson |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Aggressive paywall** | Gated a capability users already used daily, applied to the *installed base* | We taxed an existing habit. Loss aversion means removing something a user has is ~2× as painful as never granting it. The users hit hardest were our **most engaged non-payers** — the exact cohort with the highest future conversion probability and the highest review-writing propensity. | **Never take away. Price new capacity, new capability, new convenience, and new cohorts.** |
| **Intrusive ads** | Interstitials inside the core loop, shipped globally, shown to everyone including trialists and near-converters | Ratings are written by *engaged* users. Placing friction in the core loop converts your advocates into 1★ reviewers. Global rollout meant no clean read and no way to retreat without a visible reversal. | **Ads are a surface-level decision, not a product-level decision.** Segment-gated, frequency-capped, geo-staged, never in the core loop, never for payers or new users. |
| **Both** | Optimized week-1 revenue lift | Both tests were "successful" on the primary metric before the damage appeared. Uninstalls and ratings lag revenue by 2–6 weeks. | **Revenue is a fixed-horizon read; harm is a sequential read.** Different statistics, different stopping rules (§7.3). |

**The single most important reframe:** at 1.8% conversion, the problem is not that free users refuse to pay. It is that we offer *one product at one price to five different populations*. Under-2% conversion with millions of MAU is a **packaging failure**, not a willingness-to-pay failure.

---

# 2. Strategic options considered

| Option | Description | Revenue potential at M24 *(illustrative)* | Retention / ratings risk | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Harder single paywall** — raise the wall, cut free limits | Simple, fast, no new engineering | +$4–7M, decaying | **Severe.** Rerun of the failed test at larger scale. Kills the network/supply segment. | **Reject** |
| **B. Ad-monetize the free base at scale** | Treat free users as inventory | +$10–18M, but requires 3–5 ad units/session | **Severe on ratings**, and structurally caps ARPU because our DAU:MAU (26%) and session length do not support ad-primary economics | **Reject as primary; adopt as narrow, gated component** |
| **C. Segmented portfolio** (recommended) | Distinct offers per segment: two subscription tiers + group plan, usage-based passes/credits, gated low-intrusion + rewarded ads, commerce/affiliate, and B2B2C distribution | **+$20M (base) to +$26M (stretch)** | **Manageable**, because each segment gets an offer matched to its value model and no segment is coerced | **Adopt** |
| **D. Sell/exit** | Strategic sale of the user base | One-time; discount for un-monetized base | n/a | **Reject now; revisit at G3 if base case misses by >40%** |
| **E. Freemium abandonment** — go paid-only, shrink to a profitable core | Radical simplification | +$9–12M on a ~700k-user base | Kills 90% of MAU, destroys network effects, destroys acquisition funnel | **Reject; document as baseline** |

**Why C over B:** ad-primary economics require frequency we do not have. At 26% DAU:MAU and ~2.4 sessions/day for actives, our theoretical ad ceiling is roughly $1.50–2.50 ARPMAU/yr at *tolerable* ad load — real money, but not enough alone, and the incremental dollar beyond that costs ratings.

**Why C over A:** the top-decile segment is currently paying $6.99 for something they value at 3–4× that, while the bottom half is being asked to pay $6.99 for something they value at $0. Both are packaging errors, and they point in opposite directions. One price cannot fix both
[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]
